subject: Medicine
summary: Rickets is a disorder of growing bone caused by deficient mineralisation due to inadequate vitamin D, calcium, or phosphate. It presents with bone pain, deformities, and growth failure, diagnosed by clinical signs and characteristic radiographs.

sections.p: Rickets is impaired mineralisation of the growth plate in children, leading to soft, deformed bones. Diagnosis requires clinical features plus biochemical and radiographic evidence.
b: Clinical: bowed legs, wrist widening, frontal bossing
Biochemistry: low serum 25‑OH vitamin D, low/normal calcium, high alkaline phosphatase, secondary hyperparathyroidism
Radiology: cupping, fraying, and metaphyseal widening of long bones

t.b: Is vitamin D status sufficient? Low levels confirm deficiency as the primary driver of rickets
Are calcium/phosphate stores adequate? Low calcium or low phosphate points to specific aetiologies
Is there increased osteoblastic activity? Markedly elevated levels are a hallmark

sections.p: Severity is graded by radiographic scoring (e.g., Thacher score) and clinical impact on growth and deformity.
b: Mild: biochemical changes only, no visible deformity
Moderate: palpable wrist widening, mild bowing, growth deceleration
Severe: marked deformities, fractures, growth arrest

sections.p: Causes are grouped by vitamin D deficiency, phosphate deficiency, and genetic disorders; in low‑resource settings infection and malnutrition are common contributors.
b: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency (poor diet, limited sunlight)
Calcium deficiency (low dairy intake)
Phosphate loss (renal tubular disorders, Fanconi syndrome)
Genetic: X‑linked hypophosphatemic rickets, vitamin D‑dependent rickets type I/II
Secondary to chronic kidney disease or liver disease
Infections affecting absorption: HIV, TB, chronic diarrhoea, helminths

sections.p: Children present with bone pain, delayed milestones, and characteristic skeletal changes that worsen with weight‑bearing.
b: Bowed legs (genu varum) or knock‑knees (genu valgum)
Widened wrists and costochondral junction “rachitic rosary”
Frontal bossing, delayed tooth eruption
Growth faltering, irritability

sections.p: Investigations confirm deficiency, identify the underlying cause, and assess severity.
b: Basic metabolic panel, vitamin D level, PTH, urine phosphate

t.b: Is secondary hyperparathyroidism present? Elevated PTH indicates compensatory response to low calcium
Is renal phosphate wasting occurring? High ratio suggests Fanconi‑type loss
What are the radiographic hallmarks? Look for metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widening

sections.p: Unrecognised rickets can lead to permanent deformities and life‑threatening hypocalcaemia.
b: Severe hypocalcaemic seizures
Progressive deformities causing respiratory compromise
Fractures with minimal trauma

sections.p: Treat the underlying deficiency, correct biochemical abnormalities, and monitor growth and bone healing.
b: Vitamin D repletion (cholecalciferol or calcifediol) to restore 25‑OH levels
Calcium supplementation when dietary intake is low
Phosphate supplements for renal phosphate wasting
Treat underlying infection or renal disease
Physiotherapy for deformity correction

sections.p: Regular monitoring ensures biochemical normalisation and guides duration of therapy.
b: Check serum 25‑OH vitamin D and calcium every 4–6 weeks until stable
Repeat radiographs after 3–6 months to assess healing
Educate families on sunlight exposure, diet, and supplementation

sections.p: Conditions that mimic rickets must be considered to avoid misdiagnosis.
b: Osteomalacia (adult counterpart)
Renal osteodystrophy (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
Hypophosphatasia (low alkaline phosphatase)

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite active disease, especially in early stages or with concurrent illness.
b: Normal calcium with low vitamin D due to compensatory PTH rise
Elevated alkaline phosphatase in liver disease can mask bone source
Serum phosphate may be normal in early dietary deficiency

whenToSeekHelp: Severe bone pain with seizures, sudden inability to bear weight, respiratory distress from chest wall deformity, or signs of hypocalcaemic tetany

faq.q: Why can a child have normal calcium levels yet have rickets?
faq.a: Secondary hyperparathyroidism maintains serum calcium at the expense of bone, so calcium can appear normal while the growth plate remains unmineralised.

faq.q: What is the key radiographic sign that distinguishes rickets from osteomalacia?
faq.a: Rickets shows metaphyseal cupping and fraying at the growth plate, which are absent in osteomalacia because growth plates have closed.

faq.q: How does skin pigmentation affect rickets risk?
faq.a: Darker skin reduces UV‑B conversion of 7‑dehydrocholesterol to vitamin D3, increasing the likelihood of deficiency in low‑sunlight environments.

exam: Explain the pathophysiological cascade from vitamin D deficiency to secondary hyperparathyroidism in rickets.
Interpret a set of labs (low 25‑OH D, normal calcium, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH) and state the diagnosis.
Describe the radiographic features that confirm rickets and differentiate it from renal osteodystrophy.
